::: {#def-row-vector-derivative}
#### Row-vector derivative
If $f(\vb)$ is a scalar-valued function of a $p \times 1$ vector $\vb$,
such as $f(\vb) = \tp{\vx}\vb$,
then its **row-vector derivative** is:

$$
\derivf{f(\vb)}{\tp{\vb}} =
\sbmat{
\deriv{\beta_1}f(\vb) &
\deriv{\beta_2}f(\vb) &
\cdots &
\deriv{\beta_p}f(\vb)
}
$$ {#eq-row-vector-derivative}

Some sources write the same row as $\deriv{\tp{\vb}} f(\vb)$,
with the operator on the left,
as shorthand for an operator acting on $f$ rather than a matrix product
(see @rem-row-derivative-shape).
:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#rem-row-derivative-shape}
#### Which side the operator goes on

Read $\deriv{\vb}$ as a $p \times 1$ column of operators
and $\deriv{\tp{\vb}}$ as a $1 \times p$ row,
and multiply them with $f$ (a $1 \times 1$ matrix)
under the shape rule of [matrix multiplication](linear-algebra.qmd#def-matrix-mult).
The column works on the left:
$\deriv{\vb} f$ is $(p \times 1)(1 \times 1)$, a $p \times 1$ column (@def-vector-derivative).
The row does not:
$\deriv{\tp{\vb}} f$ is $(1 \times p)(1 \times 1)$,
whose inner dimensions $p$ and $1$ do not match when $p > 1$.
For the shape rule to give the $1 \times p$ row,
the operator has to go on the right of $f$, as in $(1 \times 1)(1 \times p)$.
The fraction $\derivf{f}{\tp{\vb}}$ of @eq-row-vector-derivative
avoids the question:
the transpose in the denominator says the result is a row,
without making the derivative a product.

:::
